# Power station size for a refrigerator

**For most full-size fridges, get about 1,000 Wh to cover most of a day, or about 1,500-2,000 Wh to cover a full 24 hours. The inverter should be pure sine wave with at least 1,200-1,500 W of surge.**

## The three numbers to check

1. **Running watts:** A full-size fridge draws roughly 100-250 W while the compressor is on. Almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Startup surge:** The compressor briefly spikes to about 1,000-2,400 W, depending on the fridge. Sources vary. HomeGridHQ uses 1,200 W and powerstations.reviews uses 1,300 W. This is the spec that most often makes a station fail ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so a fridge uses far less than its running watts suggest. One estimate puts a typical 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge at about 41 W average, or about 1,000 Wh a day. Allowing for inverter losses and 20% headroom, that becomes about 1,400 Wh per day ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

For your own fridge, take the kWh/year figure on the yellow EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000, and divide by 8,760 to get average watts. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average about twice the ENERGY STAR figure, and a small apartment fridge about half ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Hot kitchens and frequent door openings push usage up, so keep the door shut during the outage.

## Rough guide

| Outage length | Capacity to look for |
|---|---|
| Several hours to ~17 hrs | ~1,000 Wh |
| 24 hours | ~1,500-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh or more |

## Options named in the sources

- **About 1,000 Wh:** The [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) is listed at about $499 and ~17 hours of fridge runtime ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). The [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) has 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W output, and 2,700 W peak, at a recently seen $399-699.
- **About 2,000 Wh for a full day or more:** The [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous output, and expands up to 8,192 Wh. It lists at $899, and the code AFF5OFF takes $44.95 off. That is an affiliate link, and the store's checkout has the final word on price. HomeGridHQ estimates about 33 hours of fridge runtime for it. The [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) has 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W output, and 3,000 W peak, and is listed at $699.99 after coupon. Anker's own page makes that claim, so treat it as manufacturer marketing.

The AC180 and Jackery links go to the guide that recommends them, because the results gave no direct purchase page for those two. Prices change often and some listings were out of stock when checked, so confirm at checkout.

## Before you buy

- Use pure sine wave output, which all the stations above have. Avoid cheap modified-sine inverters.
- If you plan to run other devices like a router or lamp, add their watts and watt-hours to the totals.
- Test the setup before an outage. If the station trips when the compressor starts, unplug other AC loads and retry.

If you tell me your fridge's size and EnergyGuide kWh/year, I can narrow this to a specific capacity.
